name: Customer Discovery
description: An authored example of combining six kinds of source material into a reusable discovery playbook.
prompt: Create a new Customer Discovery collection from these sources. Combine their advice into an interview, evidence-review, and experiment playbook. Keep the source passages attached, show any disagreements, and export a pack I can share with my team.

sources.title: Ask about what actually happened
sources.route: Lectic can retrieve available English YouTube captions with optional yt-dlp. This fictional example supplies its own captions.
paragraphs: Ask the customer to describe the last time the problem occurred. Record the situation, what they tried, and what happened next.
Avoid describing your proposed solution before hearing the customer's existing workflow. A leading question can turn an interview into a pitch.

sources.title: Listen for the workaround
sources.route: Audio can be saved as an attachment. Provide a transcript for knowledge extraction; Lectic has no built-in audio transcription.
paragraphs: Ask what the person does today to work around the problem, and what that workaround costs in time, money, or effort.
Separate a compliment about an idea from evidence of a current problem. Ask for a concrete example when the answer is only a general opinion.

sources.title: Keep the observation and its context
sources.route: PDFs can be saved as attachments. Supply readable text through your assistant or another extractor; Lectic has no built-in PDF text extraction or OCR.
paragraphs: Store the participant's exact words separately from your interpretation. Keep the situation and participant context with the observation.
Count independent examples before calling something a pattern. Multiple quotes from the same person are not multiple independent observations.

sources.title: Compare the evidence before deciding
sources.route: General article URLs are saved as links. Paste the article text or supply a text file to use it as evidence.
paragraphs: Group observations by the job the person is trying to do, then compare how often the problem occurs and how costly the workaround is.
Keep contradictory observations visible. Check whether different customer contexts explain the disagreement before choosing a common recommendation.

sources.title: Write down what would change our mind
sources.route: Pasted notes and local TXT or Markdown files are supported directly. Here, the notes are explicitly supplied as source material for the playbook.
paragraphs: Before a discovery experiment, name the assumption being tested and the observation that would make the team reconsider it.
After an experiment, record the result, the decision, and the evidence behind that decision so another teammate can review the reasoning.

sources.title: Test a concrete next step
sources.route: Video files can be saved as attachments. Supply captions or a transcript for knowledge extraction; Lectic does not transcribe the video itself.
paragraphs: Choose a small experiment that tests one assumption. Define the next action and what outcome you will observe before running it.
Treat one positive response as a reason to investigate further, not proof of broad demand. Seek a concrete next step such as a scheduled follow-up or a trial.

playbook.title: Ask better interview questions
playbook.instruction: Start with a recent real event, then ask about the current workaround and its cost before discussing a solution.
playbook.example: Tell me about the last time this happened. What did you do, and how much time did it take?

playbook.title: Compare signals across sources
playbook.instruction: Keep exact observations separate from interpretations. Compare independent examples by job, frequency, and cost; retain contradictions with their context.
playbook.example: Three quotes from one participant count as one participant's evidence. Compare independent cases before deciding this is a common problem.

playbook.title: Turn findings into the next test
playbook.instruction: Choose one assumption, state what would change your mind, and run a small test with an observable next step. Save the result and decision for the team.
playbook.example: Test whether participants will schedule a follow-up. Record the result and what it changes; a positive response alone does not establish demand.
